newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU countries on track for EMU inflation goal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU countries on track for EMU inflation goal.

text.p: The European Commission issued comparable inflation data in preparation for the single currency on Friday indicating that most EU countries were on track to meet the EMU requirement on stable consumer prices.

The harmonised figures, published for the first time, showed all countries except Greece had year-on-year rates of below three percent in January. They also showed smaller gaps in inflation rates between the European Union's 15 member states.
"It is very likely that most countries are going to make this criterion," said economist Ellen van der Gulik at investment bank JP Morgan.
"If you look at the 15, the only one out is probably going to be Greece, unless you are going to see sharp movements in inflation, but that is not what we are forecasting," she said.

Depending on method used for measuring changes in annual inflation, the harmonised indices showed that either 11 or 12 member states were in line with the requirement in January, with Italy being the borderline case.
Using the year-on-year figure for January, only Spain, Greece and Portugal missed out. Italy joined them if the figure used was for a rolling 12-month average.
EU countries will be judged early next year on whether their 1997 finances have converged enough to join economic and monetary union (EMU). Price stability is one of five criteria.

The EU's Maastricht treaty states that a country's average inflation rate observed over a year should "not exceed by more than 1.5 percentage points that of, at most, the three best performing member states in terms of price stability".
JP Morgan's van der Gulik said the most striking with the new figures was that they showed smaller differences between EU inflation rates than the national price data.

"The inflation rates based on harmonised inflation are much closer together which will make it easier to meet the criterion given that it is a relative criterion, it is relative to the best performing member states," she said.

Economist Theodor Schonebeck at Deutsche Bank Research took a similar line after studying the new figures. "The inflation criterion is even less of a hurdle for qualifying for EMU than it is on the basis of national figures," he said.

The new method appeared to work in favour of countries such as Spain and Portugal, even though they were outside for now. It increased the inflation rates in the three best performing countries, thus making it easier to qualify for those with faster price rises.
"This is very good news for all Spaniards, said Maria Pilar Martin-Guzman, head of the national statistics institute INI.
The harmonised figures showed some countries with significantly different rates than previously published by their national statistics agencies as methods of compilation differ.

For example, Sweden's harmonised inflation figure amounted to 1.3 percent compared with the nationally published figure of a fall of 0.1 percent, mainly due to housing costs, and Britain's harmonised rise was 2.1 percent compared with the increase of 2.8 percent reported nationally.

The harmonised data, worked out in cooperation between the EU's statistics agency and national statistics offices, showed that Finland, Sweden and Luxembourg had the bloc's lowest inflation rates in January year-on-year -- 0.9 percent, 1.3 percent and 1.3 percent respectively.
Greece, Portugal and Spain had the highest rates -- 6.6 percent, 2.8 percent and 2.8 percent respectively.

The EU inflation rate was 2.2 percent compared with 2.7 percent a year earlier. The rate rose in eight member states, especially in Denmark and Belgium, while it fell in five, notably in Italy to 2.6 percent from 5.7 percent a year ago.
Eurostat, the statistics agency of the EU executive, said that the harmonisation process had led to quality improvements but acknowledged that further work remained to be done.

For example, because of different approaches among member states on measuring consumer prices for health, education and the cost of owner-occupied housing, these items were not yet included in the harmonised figures.
